exercise.title: Why are polar coordinates not unique?

statement.p: The pairs (r,\theta), (r,\theta+2\pi), and (-r,\theta+\pi) can name the same point. In your own words, why is that nonuniqueness both useful and dangerous, especially when two polar curves appear to miss each other?

hint.p: Adding a full turn does not move the point, and negative r plots in the opposite direction. Intersections can occur under different polar names.

exercise.title: What questions do polar coordinates answer?

statement.p: Cartesian coordinates ask how far left or right and how far up or down. In your own words, what two questions do polar coordinates ask instead, and why is that language natural for rotation, spirals, and orbits?

subsection.title: Polar graphs
subsection.p: A polar equation usually gives r as a function of \theta:
For each angle \theta, we compute the distance r, then plot the point
But there is a second way to see the same graph. Every polar equation
is automatically a parametric curve:
The angle \theta is the parameter.
This is why polar coordinates belong in the same chapter as parametric curves. A polar graph is a curve traced by a rotating ray.

example.title: the circle r=2
example.p: means that every point on the graph has distance 2 from the origin. Therefore the graph is the circle
So the polar circle is the same circle parametrization we already know.

example.title: the spiral r=\theta
example.p: says that the distance from the origin grows at the same rate as the angle.
After one full turn, the point is farther from the origin. After another full turn, it is farther still. The curve is a spiral.
This curve is called an Archimedean spiral. More generally,
has radius increasing linearly with angle.

note.title: Why polar coordinates matter
note.p: Curves involving circles, rotations, angles, or distance from a fixed point often have simple polar equations and complicated Cartesian equations.
Polar coordinates do not replace Cartesian coordinates. They give us another language, better suited to radial and angular geometry.
